lead: This unit turns a vague software idea into requirements that can be checked, built and tested. After it you can classify requirements, run elicitation, write an SRS, model use cases, classes, states and data flows, and rank requirements with quality function deployment.
about: The unit moves from requirement types to process, elicitation, validation and management, then to documents and models. 2.1 defines functional, non-functional, user, system and interface requirements. 2.2 gives the engineering process and feasibility tests. 2.3 covers stakeholders and collaborative gathering. 2.4 handles validation and change control. 2.5 writes the SRS. 2.6 builds scenarios and use cases. 2.7 adds class and behavioural models. 2.8 draws data flow diagrams. 2.9 applies quality function deployment. Each chapter feeds the next: elicitation fills the SRS, the SRS scopes models, models expose missing requirements, and QFD ranks them.

chapters.idea: A requirement is a capability or condition the software must meet; separate what it does from how well it does it.
chapters.depth: Cover functional requirements (services, inputs, outputs, exceptions), non-functional requirements (performance, security, usability, reliability, maintainability, portability), user requirements in natural language, system requirements as detailed contracts, and interface requirements to other systems. Use a classification table. Some syllabi call non-functional requirements 'quality attributes' or 'constraints'. Spend most time on FR vs NFR; keep interface specification short because only a few universities examine it separately.
chapters.figure: tree: requirements classification tree with Functional and Non-functional branches; under Non-functional show performance, security, usability; mark user and system level notes.
chapters.example: A library app must let a student search the catalogue and show results within 2 seconds; the system must store 50,000 book records; it must run on Android 8 and above; it must call a payment gateway over HTTPS. Classify each statement as functional or non-functional, and as user or system requirement. Answer: search is functional user requirement; 2 s response is non-functional performance; 50,000 records is non-functional capacity; Android 8+ is non-functional platform constraint; HTTPS payment gateway is an interface requirement.
chapters.trap: Calling a quality such as 'response within 2 s' a functional requirement; and writing a design choice ('use MySQL') as a requirement.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: what software is and why projects fail.
chapters.leave: Detailed requirement process to 2.2; SRS template to 2.5; use case and class notation to 2.6, 2.7 and Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Requirements engineering is a loop of feasibility, elicitation, analysis, specification, validation and management, not a one-time form.
chapters.depth: Cover the process stages and their outputs. Feasibility study: technical, economic, legal, operational, schedule. Show cost-benefit with simple numbers. Mention that feasibility is not a full business case. Some syllabi call the stages 'requirements development' and 'requirements management'. Keep process-model theory out; Unit 1 owns waterfall, spiral and agile.
chapters.figure: blocks: process flow Feasibility → Elicitation → Analysis → Specification → Validation, with feedback arrow from Validation back to Elicitation and a side box Management.
chapters.example: A college wants an online fee portal for 8,000 students, peak load 300 payments per hour, budget ₹6 lakh, delivery in 3 months. Check feasibility. Technical: 300/hour is about 5 payments per minute, low for a web server. Economic: ₹6 lakh must cover hardware, software, staff; compare with clerk overtime cost. Schedule: 3 months for login, payment gateway, receipt, reconciliation is tight; list a minimum scope. Operational: parents must get SMS receipts; legal: payment data must follow college audit rules. Conclude: technically feasible, economically marginal, schedule risky.
chapters.trap: Treating feasibility as only money; ignoring legal, operational and schedule feasibility.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 for requirement types; Unit 1 for life-cycle phases.
chapters.leave: Waterfall, incremental, spiral and agile models to Unit 1; full cost estimation to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Elicitation is planned conversation with all affected people, not guessing from a single manager.
chapters.depth: Cover stakeholder identification, multiple viewpoints, collaboration, first questions, interviews, workshops, focus groups, questionnaires, observation, document analysis, brainstorming and prototyping. Build a stakeholder map with interest and influence. Show a workshop agenda and conflict resolution. Some syllabi call this 'requirements gathering' or 'requirements capture'; 'capture' is misleading because users cannot hand over complete requirements.
chapters.figure: graph: stakeholder map for a rail booking system with Passengers, Booking Clerks, Finance, IT Operations, Regulator; edges labelled 'high influence' or 'high interest'.
chapters.example: For an IRCTC-style rail booking system, list stakeholders and plan a 90-minute collaborative workshop with 12 participants: 4 passengers, 3 booking clerks, 2 finance officers, 2 IT operations staff, 1 accessibility representative. Ask first questions: Who books? What fails today? What must never happen? Record conflicts: passengers want one-click booking; finance wants OTP and audit trail. Resolve by ranking: audit trail is mandatory, one-click becomes a remembered passenger profile.
chapters.trap: Listing only the paying customer; missing operators, regulators, support staff and people who maintain the system.
chapters.leave: Use case writing to 2.6; SRS wording to 2.5; interface design to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Validation checks that the right requirements are written; management keeps every change visible and traceable.
chapters.depth: Validation: reviews, inspections, prototyping, test-case generation from requirements, checklist for ambiguity, completeness, consistency, testability. Management: baseline, version, change request, impact analysis, change control board, traceability matrix, status. Only a few universities examine formal change control boards; keep that part short and use one small matrix. Distinguish validation from verification; Unit 4 owns verification detail.
chapters.figure: blocks: baseline v1.0 → change request → impact analysis → change control board → approved change → baseline v1.1; side box traceability matrix.
chapters.example: An SRS has 40 requirements. A review finds 6 ambiguous, 3 missing and 2 conflicting. A change request adds a cancellation fee: 5 modules are affected. Show the management steps. Answer: record the 11 defects; fix and re-review; baseline v1.0. For the change: log CR-01, trace to fee, booking and receipt requirements, estimate 5 modules, send to change control board, approve or reject, then release SRS v1.1. Keep a traceability row from requirement to design and test.
chapters.trap: Saying validation is testing the code; and accepting a change without impact analysis or baseline update.
chapters.leave: Verification and test execution to Unit 4; configuration management tools to Unit 5 and Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The SRS is a written contract: what the system must do, for whom, under what constraints, and how it will be judged.
chapters.depth: Cover purpose, scope, definitions, overall description, specific requirements, interfaces, performance, security, quality attributes, acceptance criteria and appendices. Use a standard IEEE-style section list; do not copy a template. Characteristics: correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent, ranked, verifiable, modifiable, traceable. Documentation techniques: numbered requirements, shall statements, tables for data, diagrams only as support. Keep it to one product example.
chapters.figure: stack: SRS sections from Introduction at top to Appendices at bottom, with Specific Requirements highlighted.
chapters.example: Write the SRS scope and five numbered requirements for a Chennai power-cut alert app for 20,000 users. It must send an alert within 30 seconds of an official outage message; cache the last 10 outages for offline viewing; run on Android 9+ and iOS 14+; let a user pick two areas; log every alert with time and area. Answer: use sections 1 Scope, 2 Overall Description, 3 Specific Requirements. Write FR-01 'The app shall show an alert within 30 s', NFR-01 'The app shall cache 10 outages', NFR-02 'The app shall run on Android 9+ and iOS 14+'.
chapters.trap: Writing design ('use Firebase') or project plan inside the SRS; and using vague words such as 'fast', 'user-friendly', 'etc.'
chapters.leave: UML diagrams to 2.6 and 2.7 and Unit 3; test plans to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A use case is a goal-driven interaction between actors and the system; a scenario is one path through it.
chapters.depth: Cover actors, primary and secondary actors, system boundary, use case diagram, main success scenario, alternate and exception flows, preconditions, postconditions, trigger and business rules. Distinguish use case from scenario and from function. Write one fully dressed use case. Some syllabi call this 'usage scenarios' or 'scenario-based modelling'. Mention includes and extends only with one example each.
chapters.figure: sequence: ATM withdrawal messages Customer → ATM → Bank for card insert, PIN, amount ₹5,000, approval, dispense, receipt.
chapters.example: An ATM cash withdrawal: customer inserts card, enters PIN, asks for ₹5,000, receives cash and receipt. Write the main success scenario and one exception. Answer: actors Customer and Bank. Precondition: card valid and ATM has cash. Main: validate card, verify PIN, check balance ≥ ₹5,000 and daily limit, debit account, dispense ₹5,000, print receipt, eject card. Exception: balance < ₹5,000 → show message, eject card, no debit. Alternate: PIN wrong three times → retain card.
chapters.trap: Drawing a use case for every screen or button; and forgetting alternate flows, which are where most exam marks sit.
chapters.leave: UML use case notation details to Unit 3; class model to 2.7; test cases from scenarios to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Class models show the things and relationships in the problem; behavioural models show how those things change state and exchange messages over time.
chapters.depth: Cover finding analysis classes (entity, boundary, control), attributes, operations, associations, multiplicity, generalization, aggregation. Data modelling: entity, attribute, relationship, cardinality. Behaviour: state machine for one class, sequence for one scenario, activity for a workflow. Keep UML notation light; Unit 3 teaches class, sequence and state diagram syntax. Some syllabi call this 'requirements modelling' or 'analysis modelling'. Add one analysis pattern such as 'information holder' only if time permits.
chapters.figure: graph: class model for hospital appointment with Patient, Doctor, Slot, Appointment; edges labelled 1..* and 0..*; Appointment has state note.
chapters.example: A hospital appointment system has 3 doctors and 30 slots per doctor per day. A patient books a slot; a doctor can cancel. An appointment moves through requested, confirmed, cancelled and completed. Identify classes, multiplicities and the state machine. Answer: classes Patient, Doctor, Slot, Appointment. Patient 1—0..* Appointment; Doctor 1—0..* Slot; Slot 1—0..1 Appointment. State machine: requested → confirmed (doctor accepts) → completed (visit done); requested → cancelled (patient or doctor cancels); confirmed → cancelled (doctor cancels).
chapters.trap: Confusing a class with an object; putting every screen field as a class; and drawing a state machine with states that are really actions.
chapters.prereq: 2.6 use cases and scenarios; Unit 3 UML notation.
chapters.leave: UML syntax and design patterns to Unit 3; database schema to a database course; test design to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A data flow diagram shows what data enters, which processes transform it, where it is stored, and where it leaves, without showing control or timing.
chapters.depth: Cover external entities, processes, data stores, data flows. Context diagram (level 0), level-1 decomposition, numbering, balancing parent and child flows. Show what DFD does not show: decisions, loops, sequence. CASE tools can check balancing and keep a data dictionary. Some syllabi call this 'flow-oriented modelling' or 'functional modelling'. Keep it to two levels.
chapters.figure: graph: level-1 DFD for rail booking with Passenger, Booking, Cancellation, Enquiry, Payment Gateway, Train Schedule store, Ticket store; edges are data flows.
chapters.example: A rail reservation system has 2 external entities (Passenger, Payment Gateway), 3 processes (Enquiry, Booking, Cancellation), and 2 data stores (Train Schedule, Ticket). Draw a context diagram and a level-1 DFD. Balance the flows. Answer: context shows Passenger sending enquiry, booking and cancellation requests and receiving train details, ticket and refund; Payment Gateway receives payment request and returns status. Level 1: Enquiry reads Train Schedule and returns train details; Booking reads Train Schedule, writes Ticket, calls Payment Gateway; Cancellation updates Ticket and requests refund through Payment Gateway. Every context flow must appear at level 1.
chapters.trap: Putting control flow or if/else decisions in a DFD; and unbalancing a child diagram by adding or losing a parent flow.
chapters.leave: UML activity and sequence diagrams to Unit 3; CASE tool commands to lab work; detailed database design to a database course.

chapters.idea: Quality function deployment turns customer needs into ranked technical responses, so engineering effort follows what customers value.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach QFD; keep it short. Cover customer needs (the 'what'), technical responses (the 'how'), importance weights, relationship matrix (9 strong, 3 medium, 1 weak, 0 none), competitive assessment and a simple weighted score. House of quality shape. Do one matrix by hand; do not add correlation roof unless the exam asks.
chapters.figure: array: house of quality matrix with rows Taste, Speed, Price; columns Menu cycle and Counter count; cells 9, 3, 1, 0; importance column 5, 3, 4.
chapters.example: A hostel mess surveys 200 students. Customer needs and importance: tasty food 5, quick service 3, low price 4. Technical responses: menu cycle and number of serving counters. Relationship strengths: taste vs menu 9, taste vs counters 1; speed vs menu 1, speed vs counters 9; price vs menu 3, price vs counters 3. Compute priorities. Answer: menu score = 5×9 + 3×1 + 4×3 = 45 + 3 + 12 = 60. Counter score = 5×1 + 3×9 + 4×3 = 5 + 27 + 12 = 44. Menu cycle ranks first.
chapters.trap: Adding every row and column without weights; and treating the relationship score as a cost or a duration.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 non-functional requirements; 2.5 SRS scope; basic multiplication.
chapters.leave: Full competitive analysis and correlation roof to a quality-management course; cost estimation to Unit 6.
